text.description: The text to insert at the cursor.

volume_level.description: Absolute level, 0..volume_max as last pushed by the server.

device.manufacturer: Google (platform); Nvidia, Sony, TCL, Hisense, onn and others (devices)
device.name: Android TV / Google TV (Android TV Remote Protocol v2)
device.notes: The same protocol the Google TV mobile app speaks, served by the Android TV Remote Service system app preinstalled on Android TV OS devices. Two TLS ports: 6467 for one-time pairing (Polo pairing protocol, pairing code shown on the TV screen), 6466 for the remote session itself (key injects, app-link launches, IME text, voice, pushed power/volume/current-app state). Discovery is mDNS _androidtvremote2._tcp.local. No authentication token or account is involved after pairing: the client certificate presented at pairing time is the credential. Amazon Fire TV is the notable exception to the whole file: it ships no Android TV Remote Service, sideloading it does not work (per the Home Assistant integration docs), and the local control path is ADB on TCP 5555, enabled by the user in Developer Options and gated by an on-screen "Allow USB debugging?" approval.

openness.notes: The pairing half is Google's own open-source Polo implementation, so that half is citation, not reconstruction. The session half (remotemessage.proto) was recovered by the community — louis49's Node implementation first, tronikos' androidtvremote2 (the Home Assistant backend) second — by watching the Google TV app; treat field names marked 'unknown' in that proto as exactly that.

upstream_docs.covers: The port-6467 pairing half only: polo.proto's OuterMessage, PairingRequest/Ack, Options, Configuration/Ack, Secret/Ack and the certificate-bound secret derivation. Google publishes this half; the RemoteMessage vocabulary on 6466 has no upstream.
upstream_docs.title: AOSP — google-tv-pairing-protocol (Polo)

upstream_docs.covers: The KEYCODE_* constants RemoteKeyCode mirrors; the authority for what each injected key means.
upstream_docs.title: Android Developers — KeyEvent

credentials.notes: Nothing is issued: the client generates its own RSA-2048 self-signed certificate (androidtvremote2 uses CN 'atvremote', 10-year validity) and pairing registers THAT certificate with the TV. Revocation is clearing the Remote Service's storage on the TV. Fire TV/ADB instead stores authorized client RSA public keys under adbd, approved via the on-screen dialog (fire_tv_adb.authentication).
stored_on_device: Paired client certificates (Android TV Remote Service storage)

factory_reset.effect: Clears accounts, installed apps, settings and every paired client certificate; the device returns to first-run setup.

steps.action: Google TV: Settings > System > About > Reset > Factory data reset. Android TV: Settings > Device Preferences > Reset. Exact menu spelling varies by manufacturer and OS version.
steps.notes: From generic Android TV documentation, not replayed against hardware; some brands also offer a physical reset pinhole.

methods.description: On-screen first-run: language, WiFi network and passphrase (or Ethernet), Google account sign-in. Performed with the bundled IR/ BLE remote; there is no provisioning protocol for a client to reimplement.

steps.action: Power on and complete the on-screen setup with the bundled remote, joining the LAN.
steps.expect: TV on the network; _androidtvremote2._tcp.local. visible to mDNS.

steps.action: Connect TLS to port 6467 presenting the client's self-signed RSA certificate, and send PairingRequest (service_name 'atvremote', client_name shown on TV).
steps.expect: PairingRequestAck, then the TV displays a 6-character hex code.

steps.action: Read the code off the TV screen and type it into the client.
Complete Options/Configuration, then send the Secret derived from both certificates and the code (androidtv_remote_v2.pairing.secret).
steps.expect: SecretAck; the client certificate is now trusted for sessions on 6466.

setup.notes: Two distinct steps, both on the device itself: joining the network (on-screen first-run, nothing to reimplement) and PAIRING each client, which is where a client has real work to do. Pairing runs once per client on port 6467 (androidtv_remote_v2.pairing has the byte-level flow): the client connects over TLS presenting a self-signed RSA certificate it generated, sends a PairingRequest, the TV shows a 6-character hexadecimal code, the user types it into the client, and the client proves it saw the code by returning a secret that binds the code to both certificates' public keys. Afterwards the client connects on 6466 with the same certificate; the TV trusts it because it paired, not because any CA signed anything. If pairing loops or errors, force-stop Android TV Remote Service and clear its storage (Settings > Apps > Show system apps > Android TV Remote Service > Storage > Clear storage), which revokes every paired client.

rejoin.notes: Re-joining WiFi is a Settings > Network operation on the TV; paired client certificates survive. A client whose TV changed address rediscovers by mDNS, not by remembered IP.

characteristics: Reference device for most community clients; voice input works, with the quirk that RemoteVoicePayload chunks smaller than 8 KB are rejected (androidtvremote2 pads to 8 KB).
If KEYCODE_POWER cannot wake it, disable Settings > Remotes & accessories > Simplified wake buttons (Home Assistant integration notes).

http_endpoints.description: Placeholder for the Android TV Remote Service, which speaks protobuf over TLS on TCP 6466 (session) and 6467 (pairing) — not HTTP. See androidtv_remote_v2 for the real wire format. Fire TV variant: the control channel is ADB on TCP 5555; see fire_tv_adb. Nothing on either port answers an HTTP GET.
http_endpoints.name: Android TV Remote Service

androidtv_remote_v2.discovery: mDNS _androidtvremote2._tcp.local.; the advertisement's SRV target port is the 6466 session port. Pairing uses the same host on 6467; there is no separate advertisement for it.
androidtv_remote_v2.framing: Every message on both ports is a protobuf varint length prefix followed by that many bytes of serialized protobuf — the google.protobuf internal varint (7 bits per byte, little-endian groups), NOT a fixed-width header and NOT gRPC framing. Messages are not delimited any other way; a TCP read may carry a partial message or several, so the varint is the only reassembly rule (androidtvremote2 base.py).

pairing.after_pairing: Close 6467. All later control is a fresh TLS connection to 6466 with the same client certificate, once per command batch or held open for a remote session.
pairing.description: Port 6467, Google's Polo pairing protocol (the one half of this file with an upstream: AOSP external/google-tv-pairing-protocol). All messages are polo.proto OuterMessage { protocol_version: 2, status: STATUS_OK, ... }. Status is an enum on the wire: 200 STATUS_OK, 400 STATUS_ERROR, 401 STATUS_BAD_CONFIGURATION, 402 STATUS_BAD_SECRET.
flow: Client -> PairingRequest { service_name: 'atvremote', client_name: <shown on the TV during pairing> }.
Client -> Options { output_encodings: [{ type: ENCODING_TYPE_HEXADECIMAL, symbol_length: 6 }], preferred_role: ROLE_TYPE_INPUT }.
Server -> Options (its own encodings; hex/6 is what TVs answer for code-based pairing).
Client -> Configuration { encoding: { type: HEXADECIMAL, symbol_length: 6 }, client_role: ROLE_TYPE_INPUT }.
Server -> ConfigurationAck. The TV now shows a 6-character hexadecimal code.
User reads the code off the screen; Client -> Secret { secret }; Server -> SecretAck { secret }. A STATUS_BAD_SECRET means the code was mistyped or expired — restart the exchange.
pairing.secret:
The code is never sent; what goes on the wire is a SHA-256 digest binding it to both endpoints. From androidtvremote2 pairing.py: sha256( hex_decode(uppercase_hex(client_cert_rsa_modulus))
        || hex_decode(uppercase_hex('0' + client_cert_rsa_exponent))
        || hex_decode(uppercase_hex(server_cert_rsa_modulus))
        || hex_decode(uppercase_hex('0' + server_cert_rsa_exponent))
        || hex_decode(code[2:6]) ), with the self-check
digest[0] == int(code[0:2], 16) — the first byte of the hash must equal the first two hex characters of the code, so the TV can reject a wrong code without another round trip. Modulus/exponent are formatted as uppercase hex WITHOUT leading zero padding before decoding. The community write-up (Aymkdn wiki) states the same construction as BigInteger byte arrays with leading null bytes stripped; the androidtvremote2 form is the one running in production Home Assistant installs.

session.description: Port 6466. All messages are remotemessage.proto RemoteMessage, a union of the fields below. On connect the SERVER speaks first.
handshake: Server -> remote_configure { code1: <feature bitmask>, device_info { model, vendor, package_name, app_version } }. code1 bits (androidtvremote2 Feature): 1 PING, 2 KEY, 4 IME, 8 VOICE, 32 POWER, 64 VOLUME, 512 APP_LINK. device_info is the first place model/vendor identity is available; mDNS does not carry it.
Client -> remote_configure { code1: <client features masked by the server's>, device_info { unknown1: 1, unknown2: '1', package_name: 'atvremote', app_version: '1.0.0' } }.
Server -> remote_set_active; Client -> remote_set_active { active: <same masked feature bits> }.

Server then pushes state, initially and on every change: remote_start { started } = power state; remote_ime_key_inject { app_info { app_package } } = foreground app (only with IME enabled); remote_set_volume_level { volume_level, volume_max, volume_muted }.
session.keepalive: When idle the server sends remote_ping_request { val1, val2 } roughly every 5 seconds and closes the connection after 3 unanswered pings; the client answers remote_ping_response { val1: <echo> }. androidtvremote2 additionally closes its own side after 16 seconds without any traffic, so a command-only client may simply connect, send, and disconnect instead of holding a session.
session.limits: No playback state (playing/paused is not reported — Home Assistant marks it assumed and pairs with the Google Cast integration for metadata), no app list (above), no wake for devices that leave the network in standby (Xiaomi boxes; TCL without 'Screenless service'; Shield without the wake-buttons setting). Power-on reachability is a hardware/standby property, not a protocol feature.

messages.remote_app_link_launch_request: field 90. { app_link: <string> } — launches whatever is registered for the link: a deep link ('https://www.netflix.com/title', 'vnd.youtube://', 'plex://') or, on devices with the Play Store, a bare package name ('com.netflix.ninja'). There is NO installed-app enumeration anywhere in the protocol: clients keep user-configured app lists (Home Assistant does exactly this), so a spec-level app picker cannot be built from the device.
messages.remote_error: field 3. Server-side error wrapper carrying the offending message.
messages.remote_ime_batch_edit: field 21. Keyboard text into the focused field: edit_info [{ insert: 1, text_field_status { start, end, value } }] with start=end=len(text)-1 and ime_counter/field_counter echoed from the server's last remote_ime_batch_edit push — the counters are what tie the edit to the field the user is looking at, so text entry requires a held session, not connect-send-disconnect. Some vendor keyboards refuse concurrent virtual keyboards and show 'use the keyboard on your mobile device' instead; disabling IME is the workaround.
messages.remote_key_inject: field 10. { key_code: RemoteKeyCode, direction: RemoteDirection } — one injected remote key. Direction SHORT (3) is a complete press+release in one message; a long press is START_LONG (1), wait, END_LONG (2). The keycode enum is the Android KeyEvent table (KEYCODE_HOME=3, BACK=4, DPAD_UP=19..DPAD_CENTER=23, VOLUME_UP=24, VOLUME_DOWN=25, POWER=26, MENU=82, SEARCH=84, MEDIA_PLAY_PAUSE=85, MEDIA_STOP=86, MEDIA_NEXT=87, MEDIA_PREVIOUS=88, MEDIA_REWIND=89, MEDIA_FAST_FORWARD=90, VOLUME_MUTE=164, INFO=165, CHANNEL_UP=166, CHANNEL_DOWN=167, TV=170, GUIDE=172, SETTINGS=176, TV_POWER=177, TV_INPUT=178, APP_SWITCH=187, ASSIST=219, SLEEP=223, WAKEUP=224, TV_INPUT_HDMI_1=243..HDMI_4=246, TV_INPUT_COMPOSITE_1=247). Whether a key DOES anything is up to the device, firmware and foreground app — Netflix ignores injected keys even from Google's own app, and TV-class codes mean nothing on a HDMI-less box.
messages.remote_set_volume_level: field 50. Server -> client volume state (level/max/muted). The client->server direction with absolute levels exists in the proto but no maintained client sends it — volume control in practice is KEYCODE_VOLUME_UP/DOWN/MUTE injects. Treated as hypothesis below.
messages.voice: fields 30-32. Send key KEYCODE_SEARCH, the server answers remote_voice_begin { session_id }; stream remote_voice_payload { session_id, samples } — 16-bit PCM, 8 kHz, mono, chunks at most 20 KB and at least 8 KB (Shield rejects smaller; pad with zeros) — then remote_voice_end { session_id }.

tls.client_certificate: Required on both ports. The client generates an RSA-2048 self-signed certificate once and reuses it forever: androidtvremote2 builds CN= 'atvremote', SHA-256 signature, basicConstraints CA:true, ~10-year validity. The certificate IS the credential: after pairing, the TV accepts sessions from certificates it paired with and closes connections from ones it did not.
tls.server_certificate: Self-signed, per-device, presented on both ports. Clients disable peer verification (verify_peer=false) and instead capture the server's public key at pairing time — the pairing secret binds to it, which is the real authentication of the server.

androidtv_remote_v2.transport_gap: Not HTTP and not SOAP. A client needs: TLS with peer verification disabled (the server certificate is self-signed and per-device), a client X.509 certificate presented on every connection, protobuf varint length-prefix framing, and the two message vocabularies below. No request/response path structure exists to hang an HTTP mapping on.

fire_tv_adb.authentication: ADB public-key auth: the client holds an RSA keypair (adbkey); the FIRST connection pops 'Allow USB debugging?' on the TV screen, and the user approves, optionally ticking 'Always allow from this computer' to persist the client's public key. No code, no account; revocation is Settings > My Fire TV > Developer Options > revoke debugging authorizations (menu spelling varies by Fire OS version).
fire_tv_adb.commands: Keys: adb shell input keyevent <KEYCODE_name|number> — the same Android keycode table as remote_key_inject (HOME=3, BACK=4, DPAD_*=19-23, VOLUME_UP=24, VOLUME_DOWN=25, POWER=26, MEDIA_PLAY_PAUSE=85, VOLUME_MUTE=164, ...), so the commands block's per-key notes double as the ADB invocation. Text: input text <escaped>. Launch: monkey -p <package> -c android.intent.category.LAUNCHER 1 (or am start with an explicit intent); stop: am force-stop <package>. State is not pushed: the androidtv library polls dumpsys for audio_state, media_session_state and wake_lock_size and applies per-app detection rules — richer than the Remote Service's surface (real playback state, running-app list) at the cost of polling.
fire_tv_adb.enablement: Off by default. On the TV: Settings > My Fire TV > Developer Options > ADB Debugging = ON. Developer Options itself is hidden on some devices until Settings > My Fire TV > About is clicked seven times, and on Fire TV Edition sets until an Amazon account is signed in. Amazon documents 5555-5585 as the acceptable port range; 5555 is what devices listen on.
fire_tv_adb.identification: After connect, identity is shell reads: getprop ro.product.model, ro.product.manufacturer, ro.serialno. Nothing pre-connection identifies a port-5555 listener as a Fire TV — treat an open 5555 as 'some Android device with ADB on', which is also why a scanner must not auto-offer it as supported hardware.
fire_tv_adb.notes: Only one ADB client session is reliably usable at a time; a second client connecting can flap the first (Home Assistant troubleshooting notes). Screenshot capture (screencap) is available over the same channel, which is how the HA integration builds album art.
fire_tv_adb.transport_gap: Same class of gap as the main protocol: the consuming app's HTTP/SOAP transports cannot open an ADB session. A client needs the ADB wire protocol (adb_shell) or an external adb server.
